ppt_outline.slide_title: Email as a Ubiquitous Communication Medium
ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Establish the prevalence and challenges of email communication in professional settings
content_points: Email dominates enterprise communication (Radicati & Levenstein, 2015)
Service providers innovate to enhance user experience across applications
Existing features: Smart Reply (Kannan et al., 2016) and SmartCompose (Chen et al., 2019)
Emerging task management tools: Gmail's Nudge and Outlook Insights

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the novel task of automated To-Do generation from emails
content_points: Novel application: Generating actionable To-Do items from email commitments
Key challenges: Email thread diversity, structural heterogeneity, and metadata complexity
Differentiation: Action-focused generation vs. traditional text summarization
Core objective: Identify task sentences, contextual information, and associated entities

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present the end-to-end framework for To-Do item generation
content_points: Two-stage process: Commitment detection followed by neural generation
Component 1: Commitment classifier identifies action-intent sentences
Component 2: Unsupervised extraction of contextual sentences
Component 3: Sequence-to-sequence architecture for final output generation

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Establish historical context for email content analysis
content_points: Pioneering works on email thread summarization (Rambow et al., 2004; Carenini et al., 2007)
Seminal research on speech act identification in emails (Carvalho & Cohen, 2005)
Cross-corpus adaptation techniques for email analysis (Azarbonyad et al., 2019)

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Highlight recent computational advances
content_points: Neural architectures for action item modeling (Lin et al., 2018)
Intent identification in email conversations (Wang et al., 2019)
Supervised approaches for email subject generation (Zhang & Tetreault, 2019)

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Identify research opportunities in email task extraction
content_points: Limited focus on task-specific summarization (Corston-Oliver et al., 2004)
Existing approaches focus on general themes rather than actionable items
Supervised methods require extensive labeled data for sentence selection

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Establish the foundational dataset used for Smart-To-Do development
content_points: Leveraged Avocado dataset (Oard et al., 2015) as core corpus
Contains anonymized Outlook mailboxes from 279 enterprise employees
Comprises 938,035 emails with rich metadata annotations
Provides structural basis for task-oriented email analysis

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Define the scope of email intents relevant to task management.
content_points: Emails contain diverse intents: meeting planning, information requests, casual conversations.
Focus on extracting 'commitment' intents where senders promise actions.
Commitments include task performance, information provision, or status updates.
Need precise identification of commitment sentences for downstream processing.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the neural architecture for commitment detection.
content_points: Binary classifier $\mathcal{C}: S \mapsto [0,1]$ operates at sentence level.
RNN-based model with word embeddings and self-attention mechanisms.
Takes full email context as input for classification decision.
Trained on 9076 annotated instances (2586 positive cases).
Achieves 86% precision and 84% recall on benchmark corpus.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Demonstrate reliability of training data.
content_points: Three-judge annotation process with majority voting.
Cohen's kappa = 0.694 shows substantial inter-rater agreement.
Dataset balance: 28.5% positive cases (2586/9076).
Gold standard derived from Avocado email corpus.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Outline the systematic process for generating annotated To-Do items from email data
content_points: Filtered 500k raw sentences through commitment classifier (confidence threshold: 0.9)
Selected 29k high-confidence candidates → 12k randomly sampled for annotation
Integrated contextual metadata (From, SentTo, Subject, Body) for each candidate
Highlighted commitment sentences to guide annotators' focus

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the human evaluation framework for generating gold-standard To-Do items
content_points: Comprehensive guidelines provided: definition, structure, and examples of ideal To-Do items
Dual-annotation system with 2 independent judges per instance
Preservation of original email vocabulary prioritized
Contextual integration of previous email thread (e_p) when available

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present quantitative insights about the annotated dataset
content_points: Final dataset: 9,349 email instances with dual annotations
Median token length = 9 (Mean = 9.71) for generated To-Do items
60.42% inter-annotator agreement on subject line utility
Human evaluation shows mean scores: 3.1 (fluency), 2.9 (completeness)

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Evaluate trade-offs in annotation quality through systematic sampling
content_points: 100-item sample evaluated on 4-point scales for fluency and completeness
Identified inverse relationship: high fluency often correlates with low completeness
Grammatical correctness vs. contextual coverage represents key tension
Case analysis demonstrates annotation challenges in action item specification

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the high-level architecture of the two-stage approach for To-Do item generation.
content_points: First stage: Sentence selection for relevant commitments.
Second stage: Generation of actionable To-Do items.
Objective: Filter out irrelevant email content (e.g., salutations, casual conversations).
Focus on informative sentences for task commitments.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the sentence selection process to identify commitment-related content.
content_points: Filters generic email content (e.g., greetings, thanks).
Identifies sentences with actionable commitments.
Leverages neural text generation for relevance scoring.
Ensures only task-relevant sentences proceed to the second stage.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Explain the sequence-to-sequence learning approach for generating structured To-Do items.
content_points: Transforms selected sentences into concise To-Do items.
Utilizes neural sequence-to-sequence models.
Achieves BLEU score of 0.23 and ROUGE score of 0.63.
First work to address To-Do generation from emails.

sections.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task

raw_result.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the unsupervised matching-based method for identifying helpful sentences in emails.
content_points: Leverage unsupervised matching to score sentences for relevance to commitment.
Define commitment sentence as query and other sentences as candidates.
Compute relevance score Ω(s_i) for each sentence based on semantic similarity.
Select top K sentences as extractive summary for commitment context.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the process of creating an enriched context for relevance scoring.
content_points: Extract top τ (τ=10) most frequent tokens from email, commitment, and subject.
Lemmatize tokens and remove stop-words for cleaner context.
Form enriched context E by concatenating commitment, subject, and top tokens.
Use enriched context to compute semantic similarity with candidate sentences.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Explain the mathematical foundation of the relevance scoring mechanism.
content_points: Compute Ω(s_i) as inner product in embedding space: h(s_i)^T h(E).
Evaluate three embedding functions: Term-frequency, FastText, and BERT.
Semantic similarity ensures alignment between enriched context and target sentence.
Subject and email topic compensate for short or less informative queries.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present empirical results comparing different embedding methods.
content_points: Measure proportion of emails with at least one helpful sentence in top K.
FastText (Max) outperforms others: 0.85 (K=2) and 0.92 (K=3).
Simple embedding methods surpass BERT without labeled supervision.
70.4% of replied-to emails contain helpful sentences in previous email body.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Describe the generation stage leveraging the identified helpful sentences.
content_points: Sequence-to-sequence model with copy mechanism for To-Do generation.
Directly copies named entities and task-specific keywords from input.
Ensures fidelity between email content and generated task.
Supports reliable task management by preserving critical information.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the core architecture of the To-Do item generation system
content_points: Problem framed as Seq2Seq learning with attention mechanisms
Encoder processes concatenated email metadata: recipient, subject, commitment sentences
Decoder generates To-Do items using attention over encoder states
Special markers distinguish different input components

ppt_outline.slide_title: Model Variants: From Vanilla to Advanced Architectures
ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Compare different model configurations for task generation
content_points: Baseline: Vanilla Seq2Seq with single LSTM encoder-decoder
Enhanced version with attention mechanism for focused context
Copy mechanism variant for preserving key entities (names, dates)
BiFocal architecture with dual encoders for query/context separation

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present empirical evaluation of model effectiveness
content_points: Copy mechanism achieves highest scores (BLEU-4: 0.23, ROUGE-L: 0.63)
Significant improvement over vanilla Seq2Seq baseline
Human judgment baseline provides competitive upper bound
Concatenation approach performs worst, validating neural design

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Examine strengths and limitations through generated examples
content_points: Successful extraction of core commitments from emails
Entity copying errors reveal model limitations (e.g., name misspellings)
Partial preservation of temporal and referential accuracy
Comparison with human-generated gold standards

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the dataset characteristics and training methodology
content_points: Dataset: 9349 email instances annotated with To-Do items
Split: 7349 training, 1000 validation, 1000 test instances
Ground-truth selection: Annotation with fewer tokens
Median encoder input length: 43 tokens (includes commitment sentence)

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present comparative model performance metrics
content_points: Evaluation metrics: BLEU-4 and ROUGE variants (F1-scores)
Human performance benchmark included
Trivial baseline: Concatenation of metadata fields
Best model: Seq2Seq with copying mechanism
Model achieves parity with human performance

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Demonstrate practical output quality
content_points: Table 3 showcases generated To-Do items
Comparative analysis of model vs human outputs
Effectiveness in capturing commitment semantics
Practical utility assessment

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Summarize core research achievements and scientific contributions
content_points: Pioneering work on automatic To-Do item generation from email context
Introduction of novel task/dataset for action-focused text intelligence
Two-stage neural framework achieves 0.23 BLEU and 0.63 ROUGE scores
First known solution for composing To-Do items from emails

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Outline promising directions for advancing the research domain
content_points: Architecture improvements for structured metadata utilization
Transition from two-stage to multi-task generation model
Joint context identification and text generation framework
Potential extensions to other productivity applications

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Summarize key contributions and provide references for further reading
content_points: Smart-To-Do: A novel application for task management over emails
First work to address composing To-Do items from emails
Two-stage process leveraging neural text generation and sequence-to-sequence learning
Achieved BLEU and ROUGE scores of 0.23 and 0.63
New dataset introduced for generating To-Do items from emails

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the concept of Smart-To-Do and its relevance in email productivity.
content_points: Email services increasingly integrate intelligent features to enhance productivity.
Smart-To-Do addresses task management by generating To-Do items from emails.
Focus on emails where senders promise to perform specific actions.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Review existing solutions and research in email productivity enhancements.
content_points: Existing tools focus on folder organization and email composition.
Limited research on automated task extraction from emails.
Gap in generating actionable To-Do items from email content.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Define the specific problem addressed by Smart-To-Do.
content_points: Automatically generate To-Do items from emails with promised actions.
Challenges in identifying and extracting actionable tasks.
Need for accurate and context-aware task generation.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Outline the two-stage process for To-Do item generation.
content_points: Leverage neural text generation techniques.
Sequence-to-sequence learning for task extraction.
Two-stage approach ensures context and action identification.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present the performance metrics of Smart-To-Do.
content_points: Achieved BLEU score of 0.23 and ROUGE score of 0.63.
First work to address To-Do item generation from emails.
Demonstrates feasibility and effectiveness of the approach.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Summarize the contributions and implications of Smart-To-Do.
content_points: Introduces a novel application for email productivity.
Pioneers task management via automated To-Do generation.
Sets a foundation for future research in email-based task automation.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Detail the neural architecture and training configurations for reproducibility
content_points: LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture with Glove embeddings initialization
Separate vocabulary for source/target sequences prevents overfitting
Training uses OpenNMT framework in PyTorch with early stopping
Validation metrics (token accuracy & perplexity) guide training decisions

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Present the empirically validated hyperparameters for best performance
content_points: Single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units
Adagrad optimizer (LR=0.15) with gradient clipping (max_norm=2.0)
Dropout (0.5) and attention dropout (0.5) for regularization
Beam search (width=5) during inference for sequence generation

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Introduce the dataset examples and the comparison methodology between human and model-generated To-Do items.
content_points: Dataset includes email threads with highlighted commitment sentences.
Comparison between human-annotated (GOLD) and model-predicted (PRED) To-Do items.
Examples demonstrate varying complexity in task extraction.
Data anonymized for privacy (names changed, sentences paraphrased).

ppt_outline.slide_title: Example 1: Partial Accuracy in Task Extraction
ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Showcase a case where the model captures the core action but misses specific details.
content_points: Sender: Beverly Evans requests action from Carlos Simmons.
GOLD: 'Forward PHP example to Beverly and Renata'.
PRED: 'Forward eCommerce PHP to Beverly'.
Model misses recipient 'Renata' and misinterprets 'PHP example'.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Demonstrate the model's ability to rephrase commitments while maintaining intent.
content_points: Sender: Kirstin Barnes commits to submitting a presentation.
GOLD: 'Submit presentation with product enhancements'.
PRED: 'Submit the enhancements for product launch'.
Model captures intent but varies in phrasing and detail.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Highlight the model's challenge in preserving contextual details.
content_points: Sender commits to updating R&D on software deployment.
GOLD: 'Keep r&d posted about deployment of software'.
PRED: 'Keep r&d posted about deployment'.
Model omits specific detail about software.

ppt_outline.slide_title: Example 4: Intent Fidelity vs. Contextual Detail
ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Illustrate the trade-off between capturing intent and contextual accuracy.
content_points: Sender: Justine Sparrow commits to informing Roma Patterson.
GOLD: 'Let Roma know result'.
PRED: 'Let Roma know about the license agreement'.
Model incorporates additional context but diverges from intended task.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Show how the model generalizes specific actions, losing precision.
content_points: Sender: Rebecca Anderson requests guidance on a bash script.
GOLD: 'Talk to John to review bash script again'.
PRED: 'Talk to John to review the activities'.
Model generalizes 'bash script' to 'activities'.

ppt_outline.slide_title: Example 6: Salient but Incorrect Information Focus
ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Demonstrate the model's tendency to focus on incorrect salient information.
content_points: Sender: Ramesh Paul commits to sending details.
GOLD: 'Send Gopal more details about tests in the desktop for v5'.
PRED: 'Send Gopal more details on presentation for the knowledge transfer'.
Model captures related but incorrect action.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Highlight the challenge of capturing contextual nuances.
content_points: Sender: Lori Howard mentions pending action on training.
GOLD: 'Let Karen know about the training provide for room reservations'.
PRED: 'Let Karen know about room reservations'.
Model omits mention of training.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Showcase a case where the model partially captures the task scope.
content_points: Sender: Matthew White commits to preparing a training plan.
GOLD: 'Put together the training plan and the overall day agenda of software training'.
PRED: 'Put together the draft agenda for software training'.
Model misses broader scope of the task.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Demonstrate the model's ability to identify implicit action items.
content_points: Sender: Diana Wilson tracks a DHL package.
GOLD and PRED: 'Let Diana know about DHL package from IBM'.
Model successfully extracts implicit task commitment.

ppt_outline.slide_purpose: Summarize the insights gained from the examples.
content_points: Model captures core actions but varies in detail preservation.
Challenges include contextual specificity and intent fidelity.
Successful in implicit task extraction but prone to generalization.
Room for improvement in comprehensive task understanding.
